title: How to read a portion
hookLine: read it, find one question, see what Rashi asks, find one thing for your life

lines: A HUNDRED VERSES ON A SUNDAY NIGHT.
YOUR EYES SLIDE OFF THE PAGE.
A WAY IN, FOR A REAL WEEK.
cards: You open the week's portion on a Sunday night with good intentions. It can be long: several chapters, sometimes over a hundred verses. By the third list of names, your eyes slide off the page.
It's normal. People have felt this for centuries, which is why they built simple ways in. You don't have to take in the whole portion at once.
You need a way of reading that fits a real week, with a job and dishes and sleep. Today, four steps that Jewish readers have used in one form or another for a very long time.

teach.h: READ IT ONCE, ALL THE WAY.
teach.b: Step one: read it. The Talmud gives a traditional minimum: read the week's portion twice in Hebrew and once in translation.
For most people today that means the English, once, all the way through, without stopping to solve anything.
Step two: find one question. Just one. Look for something odd: a word that repeats, a detail that seems unnecessary.
Try it on the moment the people reach Mount Sinai. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "they encamped in the wilderness; and there Israel encamped before the mount."
They camped, and then, in the same breath, Israel camped. Why say it twice?
Step three: see what Rashi asks. Reading the Hebrew, Rashi caught something the English hides. The first verb is plural: they camped.
The second is singular: he camped, as if the whole people were one person. Rashi explains: as one man, with one heart. And he adds a sharp little contrast.
Every other stop on the journey came with complaining and quarreling. This one didn't. Before anything could be given at that mountain, the people had to arrive as one.

teach.h: FIND ONE THING FOR YOUR LIFE.
teach.b: Step four: find one thing for your life. Maybe it's this: a family dinner, a team, a group chat the night before a big day. When did you last arrive somewhere as one, and not as a list of separate complaints?
An early teacher in the Mishnah named Ben Bag Bag said of the Torah: turn it and turn it, for everything is in it.
You don't have to turn the whole portion every week. One verse, turned well, can last seven days.

how: Many Jews prepare the weekly portion before Shabbat, some reading it twice in Hebrew and once in translation, and often with Rashi's commentary, then discuss it at the Shabbat table or in a class.

games.q: the verse says they encamped, and then Israel encamped, and in Hebrew the second verb is singular. according to Rashi, why?
o: the people camped as one, with one heart.
only Moses camped at the mountain.
games.why: Rashi: as one man, with one heart. every other stop on the journey came with complaints; this one didn't.

practice: Let one line come to mind, maybe today's, there Israel encamped before the mount, or another you remember from this path. Say it slowly, ask it one question, then let it ask you one, and don't answer quickly.
This is the verse you'll carry for the week.

wordCard.voice: Rashi, the medieval commentator whose reading of one doubled verb at Sinai, they camped, then he camped, becomes a lesson in arriving as one people.

orig.note: Hebrew: and he camped. singular, though it's said of the whole people at Sinai (Exodus 19:2).

carryVoice: Your line: one verse a week. At Sinai, it began with a people arriving as one. That's day one hundred fifty-nine.
